 Microsoft asked him to go back to India after his H-1B visa was rejected. Kunal Bahl returned, but to build Snapdeal, Titan Capital

Kunal Bahl returned, but to build Snapdeal, Titan Capital 
 Edited by Poulomi Ghosh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Nov 17, 2026, 01:49 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Kunal Bahl recalls his H-1B visa rejection story. An H-1B visa rejection in 2007 changed the course of entrepreneur Kunal Bahl's career. He was working at Microsoft in the United States and was asked to relocate to the company's India office after his work visa petition was rejected. Instead of waiting another year to reapply, Bahl decided to return to India and build his own business. Nearly two decades later, Bahl is the co-founder of e-commerce platform Snapdeal and investment firm Titan Capital. He is also a judge on Shark Tank India and has helped build two publicly listed companies. Recalling the experience in an interview with Business Insider , Bahl said the visa rejection was a blessing in disguise. "Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it," he said. Microsoft asked Kunal Bahl to move to India after H-1B rejection
 Bahl had graduated from the University of Pennsylvania, where he pursued a programme combining engineering and business. He joined Microsoft as a full-time employee in October 2006 after completing an internship with the company. But as fate would have it, his H-1B petition was rejected in June or July 2007, when he was approaching the end of his temporary work authorisation in the US. The decision came as a surprise to him, particularly because he was employed by one of the world's biggest technology companies. Microsoft offered him the option of relocating to its India office and trying for an H-1B visa again after 12 months. But Bahl decided against continuing his corporate career in India while waiting for another visa opportunity. "I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or Green Cards," he recalled. By that time, he had already been thinking about entrepreneurship and decided that if he returned to India, he would work for himself rather than continue working for Microsoft. How H-1B rejection led to Snapdeal
 Bahl contacted his high-school friend Rohit Bansal, who was then working at a financial institution, and asked whether he wanted to start a business together. The two had discussed entrepreneurship while studying together and quickly agreed to pursue the idea. Their company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before Bahl arrived in India. The founders pooled approximately $60,000 from their personal savings to get the business started. They initially launched a physical coupon-book business before moving to online couponing and eventually building Snapdeal into one of India's early e-commerce platforms. Bahl said starting a company in India in 2007 was challenging. Internet penetration and smartphone adoption were limited, digital payments were not widespread, and raising money from angel investors was difficult. The two entrepreneurs initially worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. They also stayed with their families to save on accommodation and food expenses. Their business eventually grew into Snapdeal, which became a major name in India's online shopping market. From Snapdeal to Titan Capital and Shark Tank India
 Bahl and Bansal expanded their entrepreneurial journey into startup investing in 2011 by establishing Titan Capital. Over the past 15 years, the investment firm has backed more than 320 startups, according to Bahl's Business Insider interview. Its investments include companies such as Ola and Urban Company. The founders also went on to build businesses that eventually became two publicly listed companies. Bahl is now associated with AceVector, the parent company of Snapdeal, Unicommerce and Stellaro Brands. He is also a judge on Shark Tank India, where entrepreneurs pitch their businesses to investors. Join conversation

 'No better time to come back to India'
 Looking back, Bahl described his H-1B rejection as a fortunate turning point, although he acknowledged that the experience was painful at the time. "In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous," he said, adding that it became part of a larger journey that brought him back to India to help build the country's startup ecosystem. But he admitted that returning to India is not an equally easy decision for everyone facing immigration difficulties in the US. It was easier for him to pack his bags and leave as he was unmarried. India now has widespread internet and smartphone access, a larger pool of skilled professionals, more coworking spaces, a stronger funding ecosystem and greater government support for startups. "There is no better time to come back," he said.
